title: Singapore hikes 2026 GDP growth forecast to around 6%, sees 2.5% to 4.5% growth in 2027
html:
The GDP growth forecast was raised from the 4.5% to 5.5% range projected in August by the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry on Nov 24.

ST PHOTO: LIM YAOHUI

Timothy Goh

SINGAPORE – Singapore raised its 2026 growth forecast on the back of higher AI-related production and exports, but expects the pace of performance to ease in 2027.

The gross domestic product (GDP) growth forecast has been raised to around 6% from the 4.5% to 5.5% range projected in August, the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) said on Nov 24.

In its first forecast for 2027, METI said the economy is likely to grow by a slower 2.5% to 4.5%, as the pace of investment in AI eases and most of Singapore’s key trading partners have lost momentum.

“Downside risks remain in the global economy,” Permanent Secretary for Trade and Industry Beh Swan Gin said at a media briefing on Nov 24.

He added that “concerns about the sustainability of the global AI cycle could trigger sharper corrections in global financial markets, with potential spillovers to broader economic activity”.

METI’s 2026 growth upgrade comes despite the economy growing at a slower pace of 6.1% year on year in the third quarter, down from the revised 6.4% expansion in the previous quarter. This took the growth for the first three quarters of 2026 to 6.2%.

On a seasonally adjusted quarterly basis, the economy expanded by 1.5%, moderating from the 1.8% growth in the second quarter.

The upward revision also comes despite a slowdown in the Republic’s factory output, which rose by 3.4% year on year in September, down from the 15.4% expansion recorded in August, according to data released by the Economic Development Board on Oct 26.

The figure was well below the 7.1% forecast by economists in a Bloomberg poll.

But Singapore’s non-oil domestic exports, or NODX, surged 79.8% from a year ago in October, from 68.3% in September, data from Enterprise Singapore showed on Nov 17.

Beh said: “While committed AI investments should keep AI-related demand relatively firm in the quarters ahead, the pace of growth in new AI investments is expected to moderate from its high level in 2026.”

GDP upgrade in Q3 2026

The third-quarter GDP breakdown showed that the manufacturing sector expanded by 8.5% year on year, moderating from the 13.2% growth in the previous quarter.

Growth during the quarter was driven by output expansions in the electronics, precision engineering, transport engineering and general manufacturing clusters, which outweighed output declines in the chemicals and biomedical manufacturing clusters.

In particular, robust global AI-related demand continued to support growth in the electronics and precision engineering clusters.

Meanwhile, the wholesale trade sector expanded by 14.5% year on year, accelerating from the 9.8% growth in the preceding quarter.

Growth of the sector was led by the machinery, equipment and supplies segment, which saw robust expansions in the wholesale volumes of telecommunications and computers and electronic components. This was bolstered in large part by strong global demand for AI-related electronics.

Wholesale volumes in the fuels and chemicals segment and the “others” segment, which comprises metals, timber and construction materials, household equipment and furniture, as well as food, beverages and tobacco, among others, declined during the quarter.

Wholesale volumes in the fuels and chemicals segment were affected by oil supply disruptions caused by the Middle East conflict.

METI said the August GDP upgrade was based on the fact that the economic impact of the Middle East conflict had been less severe than initially projected, while the global AI investment boom was expected to provide significant tailwinds to growth.

Since then, AI-related production and exports, driven by a stronger-than-expected buildout of data centres, have continued to accelerate. The momentum is expected to continue for the rest of the year.

The ministry also noted that although elevated energy prices have contributed to global inflationary pressures and tighter monetary policy in several economies, its assessment, on balance, is that the Republic’s external demand outlook for the year has improved from its August assessment.

Against this backdrop, Singapore’s GDP growth outlook for the rest of 2026 remains firm.

Strong global AI-related demand will continue to drive growth in the manufacturing and wholesale trade sectors, while growth in outward-oriented services sectors such as finance and insurance, and information and communications, should remain resilient.

Meanwhile, growth in the accommodation sector will be supported by strong hotel bookings amid a robust line-up of events. However, the outlook for the retail trade and food and beverage services sectors remains subdued.

Outlook for 2027

Looking ahead to 2027, METI said US GDP growth is expected to ease as restrictive monetary policy and weaker real wage growth weigh on investment and consumption, while the pace of AI investments is projected to moderate.

China’s economy is also expected to slow as export growth softens amid moderating global AI-related demand and sluggish consumption growth.

METI also flagged other downside risks to the global economy.

A further escalation of the conflict in the Middle East could lead to fresh spikes in the prices of energy commodities and other key intermediate inputs. The rise in inflationary pressures and resulting tighter global financial conditions could dampen global growth.

Economic and political uncertainties in external economies could also weigh on investment and consumption in these economies.

Beh said that against this backdrop, Singapore’s GDP growth is projected to moderate in 2027.

In particular, the pace of expansion of the electronics and precision engineering clusters of the manufacturing sector and the machinery, equipment and supplies segment of the wholesale trade sector is expected to “moderate from the high levels recorded in 2026”.

“However, the projected recovery in global oil supply is likely to support a modest pickup in petroleum output in the chemicals cluster and wholesale volumes in the fuels and chemicals segment of the wholesale trade sector,” he said.

On the other hand, consumer-facing sectors such as retail trade and food and beverage services may be “weighed down by the continued shift in local spending abroad in tandem with a sustained increase in outbound travel”.

Jester Koh, associate economist at UOB, said the upcoming Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link could encourage more Singaporeans to cross the border for lower-cost groceries and dining.

“However, this may be partly offset by stronger visitor spending from Johoreans in Singapore,” he said.

OCBC chief economist Selena Ling said the technology upcycle has given Singapore a much larger growth lift than initially anticipated, with the benefits extending beyond electronics manufacturing into precision engineering, wholesale trade and financial services.

“The revised data suggests that this impulse has been stronger and more persistent than initially envisaged,” she said.

The expected slowdown in growth should also be viewed primarily as “normalisation from an exceptionally strong base rather than evidence of an impending downturn”.

“The key swing factor will remain the durability of the AI investment cycle, especially given recent market gyrations and incoming US policy measures,” said Ling. “Our base case remains one of slower but still relatively firm growth in 2027, rather than a hard landing,” she added.
summary: Singapore raises 2026 GDP growth forecast to around 6% on strong AI-related exports and production, while 2027 growth is seen easing. Read more at straitstimes.com.
